discussion: Red-versus-green status dots are invisible to many users; when this setting is on, add glyphs, patterns, or text so the distinction survives without hue. It maps to the system Differentiate Without Color switch, and honoring it usually improves the design for everyone.
name: accessibilityDifferentiateWithoutColor
summary: True when the user asks interfaces to convey meaning through shape and symbols rather than color alone.

discussion: System video players dim detected flash sequences automatically when this setting is enabled; apps with custom playback pipelines should read the flag and either apply their own mitigation or warn before strobe-heavy content. It joined the accessibility environment values in the 2023 cycle.
name: accessibilityDimFlashingLights
summary: True when the user asks that video with flashing or strobing effects be dimmed during playback.

discussion: This is a broader signal than the per-technology flags: it is true for VoiceOver, Switch Control, and similar tools. Unusually for an environment value, it is settable, which UI tests and previews exploit to force accessibility-active code paths. Use the specific flags when behavior should differ by technology.
name: accessibilityEnabled
summary: Indicates whether an assistive technology that reads the accessibility tree is currently active.

discussion: Smart Invert flips UI colors but expects apps to protect imagery; photos, video, and brand artwork should be marked or handled so they are not inverted into negatives. Reading this flag lets custom-rendered content such as Canvas drawings pick palettes that remain sensible under inversion.
name: accessibilityInvertColors
summary: True when the system is displaying colors inverted, typically via Smart Invert.

discussion: This reflects the system-wide Play Animated Images setting introduced in the 2023 accessibility pass. Apps that render their own animated image formats should show a still first frame with an explicit play control when the value is false, since only system components respect the setting for free.
name: accessibilityPlayAnimatedImages
summary: False when the user has asked that animated images like GIFs not play automatically.

discussion: System materials handle this automatically by turning opaque, but hand-rolled translucent overlays, glass cards, and custom vibrancy need to check the flag themselves. Swapping a material for a solid fill when it is on preserves legibility for users who find blurred layers hard to parse.
name: accessibilityReduceTransparency
summary: True when the user prefers opaque backgrounds instead of blur and translucency effects.

discussion: Borderless text buttons can be indistinguishable from labels; with this setting on, apps should add underlines, borders, or filled backgrounds so tappable things look tappable. System button styles respond automatically, so the flag matters mainly for custom ButtonStyle implementations.
name: accessibilityShowButtonShapes
summary: True when the user asks buttons to display visible shapes such as underlines or bordered backgrounds.

discussion: Switch Control users step through focusable elements sequentially, so interfaces with dozens of tiny targets become fatiguing; this flag lets you consolidate actions into fewer, larger controls when it is on. Like the VoiceOver flag, it should adjust interaction economics, not hide functionality.
name: accessibilitySwitchControlEnabled
summary: True while Switch Control is actively scanning the interface for switch-based navigation.

discussion: Most VoiceOver support should come from proper labels and traits rather than branching, but this flag is legitimate for behavioral swaps: pausing auto-advancing carousels, extending toast durations, or replacing hover-revealed controls with always-visible ones. Reacting to it via onChange also lets you re-announce important state when the reader starts.
name: accessibilityVoiceOverEnabled
summary: True while the VoiceOver screen reader is running.

children.name: Image.DynamicRange.standard
children.summary: Clamps image rendering to SDR brightness, so HDR photos tone-map down instead of glowing past neighboring UI.

children.name: Image.DynamicRange.constrainedHigh
children.summary: Allows some HDR headroom while capping peak brightness, a good compromise for photos shown alongside text and controls.

children.name: Image.DynamicRange.high
children.summary: Lets an image use the full HDR range the display supports, appropriate for a dedicated full-screen photo view.

code:
PhotoGrid(photos: photos)
    .allowedDynamicRange(.constrainedHigh)

PhotoDetail(photo: selected)
    .allowedDynamicRange(.high)
discussion: HDR photos can bloom brighter than surrounding UI, which is often unwanted in mixed layouts like grids; writing a constrained range keeps highlights in check while a photo detail view can allow full HDR. The value is an optional Image.DynamicRange, with nil deferring to system policy.
name: allowedDynamicRange
summary: The image dynamic range (standard, constrained high, or high) permitted for content in this environment.

code:
Text("Estimated arrival: 12 minutes")
    .lineLimit(1)
    .allowsTightening(true)
    .truncationMode(.tail)
discussion: Tightening is a gentler first resort than scaling or truncation: the system pulls letters marginally closer to rescue a line that barely overflows. It is off by default, and the .allowsTightening() modifier writes the flag into the environment for everything beneath it.
name: allowsTightening
summary: Whether text may compress inter-character spacing slightly to fit a line before truncating.

discussion: Introduced as the modern replacement for the macOS-only controlActiveState, this single Bool answers the question most views actually ask: should I draw at full strength or dimmed because my window is in the background. It reads naturally in cross-platform code since it exists everywhere and simply stays true on platforms without background windows.
name: appearsActive
summary: A Boolean indicating whether the enclosing window should render its content with an active appearance.

discussion: Codes, usernames, and search fields for exact identifiers are the classic places to disable correction, and doing it through the environment covers every field in a form at once. The value began life as disableAutocorrection and was renamed to read positively; the modern modifier is .autocorrectionDisabled().
name: autocorrectionDisabled
summary: Whether text input views in this environment should suppress autocorrection suggestions.

discussion: When you background a container with a blur material, SwiftUI records it here so descendant content can switch to vibrant rendering that stays legible over the blur. Reading the optional Material tells a reusable component whether it sits on glass and should, for example, prefer hierarchical foreground styles over hard-coded colors.
name: backgroundMaterial
summary: The material, if any, that an ancestor placed behind the current view's subtree.

children.name: BackgroundProminence.standard
children.summary: The everyday case: the view sits on an ordinary background, so tinted and accent-colored foregrounds read normally.

children.name: BackgroundProminence.increased
children.summary: Reported inside a selected list row and similar emphasized surfaces, where accent-colored foregrounds would vanish into the highlight.

discussion: When a List row is selected with the accent-colored highlight, content inside it receives an increased background prominence, and tinted text or icons that would vanish against the accent color should switch to white or primary. Reading this value is how custom row accessories match the automatic behavior of Text and Label.
name: backgroundProminence
summary: Signals when a view sits on a prominent background, such as a selected list row, so foreground colors can adapt.

code:
Image(systemName: "battery.100percent.bolt")
    .symbolRenderingMode(.palette)
    .foregroundStyle(.white, .green)
    .backgroundStyle(.green.gradient.opacity(0.3))
discussion: Written by the .backgroundStyle() modifier, this value feeds the .background shape style that multi-layer SF Symbols and some system controls use for their backdrop layer. It is type-erased to AnyShapeStyle, so gradients and materials work as well as flat colors.
name: backgroundStyle
summary: An optional shape style that fills the background layer of symbols and styled content in this environment.

children.name: ButtonRepeatBehavior.automatic
children.summary: Defers to the platform, which repeats only for controls that conventionally do so rather than for every button.

children.name: ButtonRepeatBehavior.enabled
children.summary: Turns a press-and-hold into a stream of action invocations, ideal for nudging a value up or down.

children.name: ButtonRepeatBehavior.disabled
children.summary: Explicitly opts a button out of repeating even when an ancestor enabled it, such as a reset action inside a repeat-enabled toolbar.

discussion: Enabling repeat turns an ordinary Button into a press-and-hold stepper, firing the action at an accelerating cadence, which suits increment controls and media scrubbing. The .buttonRepeatBehavior() modifier writes the value, and custom PrimitiveButtonStyle implementations can read it to honor the same contract.
name: buttonRepeatBehavior
summary: Whether buttons in this environment repeatedly trigger their action while held down.

discussion: AppKit conventions dim window chrome and controls when a window loses key status, and this value let SwiftUI views on the Mac follow suit with cases like key, active, and inactive. It was deprecated in the 2024 cycle in favor of the simpler cross-platform appearsActive Bool. Use it only when targeting older macOS releases.
name: controlActiveState
summary: Reports whether the containing macOS window is key, merely active, or inactive so controls can dim appropriately.

discussion: Wheel pickers on the watch size their rows from this environment metric, and custom item views can read it to align decorations with the selection band. Writing a larger value through .environment() gives chunkier rows for glanceable pickers like timer durations.
name: defaultWheelPickerItemHeight
summary: The standard row height for items in wheel-style pickers on watchOS.

children.name: DocumentConfiguration.fileURL
children.summary: The optional on-disk location of the open document, nil for a new file that has never been saved.

children.name: DocumentConfiguration.isEditable
children.summary: False when the document was opened read-only, letting your editor lock its controls instead of failing at save time.

discussion: Views inside a document scene often need the on-disk location for features like Reveal in Finder or a title bar subtitle, and this optional configuration exposes fileURL plus whether the document opened editable. It is nil outside document-based scenes, making it a cheap way to detect that context.
name: documentConfiguration
summary: Describes the document backing the current DocumentGroup scene, including its file URL and editability.

discussion: Increased prominence renders List section headers in bold, larger type, matching the sectioned look of apps like Settings' subpages. The .headerProminence() modifier sets it per section or per list, and custom container styles can read the Prominence value to draw their own headers consistently.
name: headerProminence
summary: The visual weight (standard or increased) that section headers in this environment should adopt.

children.name: Image.Scale.small
children.summary: Shrinks symbols below their text-relative default, handy for dense captions and inline badges.

children.name: Image.Scale.medium
children.summary: The baseline scale where a symbol sits in proportion to the cap height and weight of the surrounding font.

children.name: Image.Scale.large
children.summary: Enlarges symbols relative to the font, giving toolbar and empty-state glyphs extra presence without changing the text size.

discussion: This value controls how SF Symbols and other template images scale relative to surrounding text, and it is written by the .imageScale() modifier on any ancestor. Because it travels through the environment, a toolbar or list style can bump every symbol up or down without touching individual Image views. It only affects symbol-like images; fixed-size bitmaps ignore it.
name: imageScale
summary: The relative size (small, medium, or large) applied to symbol images within the current environment.

discussion: On Apple Watch this flips when the wrist drops and the always-on display takes over; well-behaved apps thin out bright fills, hide per-second updates, and avoid large white regions. The same signal drives iPhone StandBy night dimming. Combine it with TimelineView so update frequency drops along with luminance.
name: isLuminanceReduced
summary: True when the display is in a dimmed always-on state, asking content to reduce brightness and detail.

discussion: The .scrollDisabled() modifier flips this flag for every ScrollView, List, and TextEditor beneath it, which is handy when embedding a scrollable control inside a paging container that should own the gesture. Programmatic scrolling and layout are unaffected; only interactive scrolling is gated.
name: isScrollEnabled
summary: Whether scrollable containers in this environment respond to user-initiated scrolling.

discussion: A nil value means unlimited, and any ancestor's .lineLimit() call narrows it for the subtree. Custom text-heavy components can read the limit to decide whether to offer a Show More affordance, since the environment tells them the constraint without measuring.
name: lineLimit
summary: The optional maximum number of lines that text in this environment may occupy.

discussion: Unlike font line height, this is purely additive space between adjacent lines, and zero is the default. Long-form reading views often set it once on their container so every paragraph, caption, and quote below shares the same rhythm.
name: lineSpacing
summary: The extra vertical distance, in points, inserted between lines of wrapped text in this environment.

discussion: Injected at the app root with .environment(\.managedObjectContext, container.viewContext), this value is what @FetchRequest silently reads to execute its query. Views mutate and save through the same context so undo grouping and merge policies stay coherent. It predates SwiftData, which replaces this pattern with modelContext.
name: managedObjectContext
summary: The Core Data managed object context that fetch requests and data mutations in this view hierarchy use.

children.name: MaterialActiveAppearance.automatic
children.summary: Materials follow the window: vivid while it is key, muted once it drops into the background.

children.name: MaterialActiveAppearance.active
children.summary: Keeps materials at full strength even in a deactivated window, which a floating media or status panel may want.

children.name: MaterialActiveAppearance.inactive
children.summary: Renders materials in their dimmed form regardless of window state, useful for previews or intentionally recessed chrome.

children.name: .materialActiveAppearance(_:)
children.summary: The modifier that writes this value for a subtree, decoupling material vividness from the window's activation state.

code:
SidebarArtwork(item: nowPlaying)
    .background(.regularMaterial)
    .materialActiveAppearance(.active)
discussion: Materials normally desaturate when their window deactivates; this value overrides that coupling, so a media sidebar can stay vivid in background windows or a preview can deliberately show the inactive look. Write it with the matching .materialActiveAppearance() modifier and read it in custom chrome that mimics material behavior.
name: materialActiveAppearance
summary: Controls whether materials in this environment render in their active or inactive (dimmed) appearance.

children.name: MenuOrder.automatic
children.summary: Lets the system choose an ordering, which on iOS may flip the items so the first one lands nearest the presenting control.

children.name: MenuOrder.fixed
children.summary: Guarantees items appear top-to-bottom exactly as declared, which matters when the sequence itself carries meaning.

children.name: MenuOrder.priority
children.summary: Places the earliest items closest to where the menu originates, mirroring the system's proximity-based reordering.

discussion: iOS sometimes reverses menu items so the first action lands nearest the user's finger; MenuOrder lets you read or pin that behavior with cases like fixed and priority alongside automatic. The .menuOrder() modifier sets it for a subtree, and custom menu-like components can read the value to match platform behavior.
name: menuOrder
summary: The preferred ordering strategy for items in menus presented from this environment.

discussion: A value of 1 forbids shrinking; 0.5 lets text compress to half size to avoid an ellipsis. It travels through the environment so a row of stat tiles can share the same shrink policy, keeping mixed-length numbers visually consistent. Combine it with a line limit, since unconstrained text simply wraps instead of scaling.
name: minimumScaleFactor
summary: The smallest fraction of the original font size that text may shrink to before truncating.

discussion: This TextAlignment value only matters once text wraps: single-line text is positioned by its frame, but the second and later lines follow this alignment. It flows down the environment from the .multilineTextAlignment() modifier, so a whole card layout can center its wrapped copy with one line at the container level.
name: multilineTextAlignment
summary: The environment value backing multiline text alignment, controlling how wrapped lines align within a Text view.

discussion: Before this existed, opening the settings window from a button required AppKit selectors; the OpenSettingsAction makes it a one-line call that finds or creates the Settings scene. SettingsLink wraps the same behavior as a ready-made control, so reach for this action when the trigger is not a simple button, such as an onboarding flow ending in configuration.
name: openSettings
summary: A macOS action that opens the app's Settings scene programmatically.

children.name: PurchaseAction.callAsFunction(_:options:)
children.summary: Starts StoreKit's confirmation sheet for a product, optionally with purchase options like quantity, and suspends until the user finishes or backs out.

children.name: Product.PurchaseResult
children.summary: The enum the action returns: a success carrying a verification result, a pending state awaiting approval, or a user cancellation.

children.name: Product.PurchaseOption.appAccountToken(_:)
children.summary: Tags the transaction with a UUID from your own account system so server-side receipts can be tied back to the buyer.

discussion: This PurchaseAction lets fully custom paywalls start transactions without embedding StoreKit's prebuilt views, presenting the system confirmation sheet from the current scene. It is async and throwing, returning a PurchaseResult you inspect for success, pending, or cancellation. Purchase options such as quantity or promo offers pass through the call.
name: purchase
summary: A StoreKit action that initiates the purchase flow for a Product from any view.

discussion: This is the plumbing behind RenameButton: the button simply invokes whatever action an ancestor registered with .renameAction(). Reading the value yourself lets a context menu item or keyboard shortcut start the same rename flow, typically focusing a text field. It is nil when no rename behavior has been configured.
name: rename
summary: An optional RenameAction that triggers the rename handler defined by a renameAction modifier higher in the hierarchy.

children.name: SearchSuggestionsPlacement.automatic
children.summary: The default request, which resolves to a menu or the content area depending on platform and where the search field lives.

children.name: SearchSuggestionsPlacement.menu
children.summary: Suggestions drop down as a compact menu beneath the field, typical of a macOS toolbar search.

children.name: SearchSuggestionsPlacement.content
children.summary: Suggestions take over the main content region, the iOS pattern where the results list gives way to a suggestion list.

children.name: SearchSuggestionsPlacement.Set
children.summary: An option set of placements used with searchSuggestions(_:for:) to show or hide suggestions only in specific locations.

discussion: The same searchable view hierarchy can surface suggestions differently by platform and container: a toolbar search field on macOS shows a menu, while iOS replaces the content area. Reading this value inside the suggestions builder lets you provide compact rows for menu placement and richer cells for content placement.
name: searchSuggestionsPlacement
summary: Where the current context displays search suggestions, such as inline menu or dedicated content area.

discussion: Since the 2023 widget redesign, the same widget renders both with and without its containerBackground depending on context. When this is false, content should expand into the reclaimed padding and avoid drawing its own competing backdrop. Pair it with widgetContentMargins for exact spacing.
name: showsWidgetContainerBackground
summary: Whether the widget's container background is currently visible, which it is not in contexts like StandBy or the watch smart stack.

discussion: Corner complications on watch faces can render a curved label supplied by the widgetLabel modifier; this flag tells the view whether that label is actually being shown so it can drop duplicate text from its main body. It keeps the same widget code correct across corner, circular, and inline placements.
name: showsWidgetLabel
summary: True when a watchOS accessory widget has an attached text label, as on the corner complication slots.

discussion: This was the first-generation way to read the user's preferred text size, exposing the UIKit-style ContentSizeCategory enum. Apple deprecated it in the 2021 cycle in favor of dynamicTypeSize, whose cases are comparable with range operators and easier to branch on. Existing code still compiles, but new code should not adopt it.
name: sizeCategory
summary: The original Dynamic Type content size category value, superseded by dynamicTypeSize.

children.name: SpringLoadingBehavior.automatic
children.summary: Leaves spring loading to platform defaults, which enable it only for system controls that conventionally support it.

children.name: SpringLoadingBehavior.enabled
children.summary: Marks a control as a spring-loading target: pausing a drag over it flashes and activates it so users can navigate mid-drag.

children.name: SpringLoadingBehavior.disabled
children.summary: Prevents a control from triggering during drag hover, even inside a container that enabled the behavior.

code:
NavigationLink("Projects", value: Folder.projects)
    .springLoadingBehavior(.enabled)
    .dropDestination(for: DocumentItem.self) { items, _ in
        move(items, to: .projects)
    }
discussion: Spring loading is the drag-and-drop nicety where hovering a dragged item over a navigation link or button briefly flashes it and then activates it, letting users drill into a destination mid-drag. The behavior is opt-in per subtree through the .springLoadingBehavior() modifier, and this value exposes the setting to custom controls.
name: springLoadingBehavior
summary: Controls whether controls in this environment spring-load, activating when a drag hovers over them.

children.name: SymbolRenderingMode.monochrome
children.summary: Draws every layer of a symbol in a single foreground style, the flat default look.

children.name: SymbolRenderingMode.hierarchical
children.summary: Applies one color at graduated opacities per layer, adding depth from a single shape style.

children.name: SymbolRenderingMode.palette
children.summary: Assigns a distinct shape style to each symbol layer, taken from the multiple arguments passed to foregroundStyle.

children.name: SymbolRenderingMode.multicolor
children.summary: Uses the colors baked into the symbol itself, such as the yellow sun in weather glyphs.

discussion: The .symbolRenderingMode() modifier writes here, and every SF Symbol below inherits the mode unless overridden. Reading the optional value is useful in custom label styles that need to decide how many foreground styles to supply, since palette mode consumes multiple styles while monochrome uses one.
name: symbolRenderingMode (environment)
summary: The environment slot holding the symbol rendering mode (monochrome, hierarchical, palette, or multicolor) for this subtree.

discussion: Containers use this to restyle symbols wholesale: tab bars on iOS famously request the fill variant of every item's icon this way. The .symbolVariant() modifier composes values into the environment, and Image resolves the final symbol name from the combination, so you can write plain base names like heart and let context choose heart.fill.
name: symbolVariants
summary: The symbol variant (fill, circle, slash, and so on) that SF Symbols in this environment resolve to.

children.name: TabViewBottomAccessoryPlacement.inline
children.summary: The accessory has collapsed into the tab bar strip, so only a slim single-row layout fits.

children.name: TabViewBottomAccessoryPlacement.expanded
children.summary: The accessory floats above the full tab bar with room for artwork, a scrubber, and secondary controls.

children.name: .tabViewBottomAccessory(content:)
children.summary: Attaches the accessory view to a TabView; the placement value is delivered to that content as the bar collapses and expands.

discussion: With the 2025 design, a bottom accessory like a mini player can collapse into the tab bar region as the user scrolls; this optional placement value is read inside the accessory content to swap between a compact inline rendering and the full expanded one. It complements tabBarMinimizeBehavior, which controls when the collapse happens.
name: tabViewBottomAccessoryPlacement
summary: Tells a TabView bottom accessory whether it is currently inline with the collapsed tab bar or expanded above it.

children.name: Text.Case.uppercase
children.summary: Renders text in capitals at draw time, the same transform Form section headers apply on iOS.

children.name: Text.Case.lowercase
children.summary: Forces lowercase rendering, useful for stylized labels or normalizing user-typed handles for display.

discussion: Form section headers on iOS historically uppercase themselves through exactly this mechanism, and passing nil with .textCase(nil) is the well-known trick to stop them. The transform applies at render time, leaving the underlying string untouched, so accessibility and copy operations still see the original casing.
name: textCase
summary: An optional transform that forces text in this environment to render uppercased or lowercased.

children.name: Text.TruncationMode.head
children.summary: Drops characters at the beginning so the ending stays visible, right for serial numbers and IDs whose suffix identifies them.

children.name: Text.TruncationMode.middle
children.summary: Removes the center of the string so both the start and the end survive, the standard treatment for file paths.

children.name: Text.TruncationMode.tail
children.summary: The default: cuts the string at the end and appends an ellipsis.

discussion: Middle truncation is the classic choice for file paths, where both the start and the extension matter, and setting it via the environment lets a whole column of labels share the behavior. The .truncationMode() modifier writes this value, and Text consults it whenever line-limited content overflows.
name: truncationMode
summary: Determines where Text drops characters when a line cannot fit: at the head, middle, or tail.

discussion: With automatic margins enabled, the system pads widget content differently per platform and context; this EdgeInsets value reveals those margins so a view can extend selected elements, like a full-bleed map, to the true edge while keeping text inside the safe region. It complements the contentMarginsDisabled widget configuration modifier.
name: widgetContentMargins
summary: The default content insets the system applies around widget content in the current context.

children.name: WidgetFamily.systemSmall
children.summary: The square Home Screen size; systemMedium and systemLarge are its wider and taller siblings.

children.code:
StaticConfiguration(kind: "Stats", provider: Provider()) { entry in
    StatsWidgetView(entry: entry)
}
.supportedFamilies([.systemSmall, .systemMedium, .systemLarge, .systemExtraLarge])
children.name: WidgetFamily.systemExtraLarge
children.summary: The oversized rectangular family offered on iPad Home Screens, roomy enough for multi-column layouts.

children.name: WidgetFamily.accessoryRectangular
children.summary: The Lock Screen and watch rectangular slot, rendered vibrant or accented; accessoryCircular and accessoryInline are its companions.

children.name: WidgetFamily.accessoryCorner
children.summary: A watchOS-only family that curves around a watch face corner and can carry a widgetLabel.

discussion: A single widget view typically serves several families, and this value is how it branches between a glanceable small layout and a data-rich large one. Accessory families added for the Lock Screen and watch complications also arrive through the same enum, so exhaustive switches future-proof the layout.
name: widgetFamily
summary: The widget size family (small, medium, large, or an accessory style) that the current widget view is rendering for.

children.name: WidgetRenderingMode.fullColor
children.summary: The standard Home Screen presentation where every color you specify is drawn exactly as given.

children.name: WidgetRenderingMode.vibrant
children.summary: Used on the Lock Screen and in StandBy, where content is desaturated and blended with the wallpaper, so hue carries no meaning.

children.name: WidgetRenderingMode.accented
children.summary: A two-tone treatment on watch faces and tinted Home Screens: accentable views take the accent color and everything else renders neutral.

children.name: .widgetAccentable(_:)
children.summary: Flags a view and its descendants to receive the accent tint whenever the widget renders in accented mode.

discussion: Lock Screen widgets render vibrant (desaturated over the wallpaper) and watch complications can render accented, both of which flatten custom colors; reading this mode lets the view drop color-coded meaning and lean on opacity hierarchies instead. StandBy and tinted Home Screens make handling non-full-color modes increasingly important.
name: widgetRenderingMode
summary: How the system is rendering the current widget: full color, vibrant, or accented.
